solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Seabird left mother when covered with hairy coat

indicators.note: something covered is wrapped on the outside, so one piece goes round the rest

parts.note: an animal's hairy coat is its fur
L is the standard abbreviation for left
MA is an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: A seabird abandons its mother once it has grown a shaggy coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' reads as a verb, abandoned, but it is the direction abbreviation; 'when' merely links the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: The fulmar is a grey and white petrel of northern oceans, a familiar bird of British sea cliffs.

clue.text: One looks ahead, following posh traveller missing nothing

indicators.note: missing means going without, so the zero-shaped letter is dropped from the word
this word is itself a source of letters here, the usual abbreviation used in page references

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for following, as in 'p. 12f'
U means upper-class, as in 'U and non-U' usage
a tourist is someone travelling for pleasure
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A forward-looking person trails behind a well-to-do tourist who has forgotten nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' looks like a position word, but it is F; U for posh (upper-class) is a crossword convention. TOURIST loses its O to make TURIST.
explanation.definitionFit: A futurist is someone who studies and predicts coming trends, literally a person whose gaze is fixed on tomorrow.

clue.text: Alcoholic drink by freezer that's used as a flavouring

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for the noun: something used as a flavouring

parts.note: liquor is strong alcoholic drink
ice is what freezes a drink, loosely a freezer

explanation.surface: A spirit served next to the ice tray turns out to be a flavouring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' simply places the second piece beside the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Liquorice root extract gives its sweet, aniseed-like taste to sweets, drinks and tobacco, so it is a common flavouring agent.

clue.text: Greedy Victor claiming benefit? On the contrary

indicators.note: to claim something is to take hold of it, so one piece grips another
this flips the stated roles, so the holder becomes the thing held and vice versa

parts.note: aid is help or benefit
Victor is V in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A grasping man named Victor tries to claim welfare payments.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, V would hold AID; 'On the contrary' reverses the roles so AID holds V: A(V)ID.
explanation.definitionFit: Avid means eager or keen, and in its older sense hungry or grasping for more, which is greed.

clue.text: Party with gold cracker announced — a guest might activate it outside

definitions.text: a guest might activate it outside

parts.note: a do is an informal party
or is gold in heraldry

indicators.note: something announced is spoken out, so we go by what the word sounds like

parts.note: a cracker is an attractive woman, a belle

explanation.surface: A party with a gold Christmas cracker is announced, which a visitor might pull outside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracker' suggests Christmas crackers, but it is British slang for a stunning woman, a belle. OR for gold comes from heraldry.
explanation.definitionFit: A visitor standing at the front door presses the doorbell to let the household know someone has arrived.

clue.text: Awkward antihero being broadcast

indicators.note: something awkward is ungainly and out of order, so the letters get rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An awkward, unheroic protagonist is the subject of a broadcast programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awkward' seems to describe the antihero, but it signals the rearrangement of all eight letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Radio and television programmes are said to be on the air while they are actually being transmitted live.

clue.text: One deletes type of music which The Beatles recorded

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the album it describes

parts.note: a rubber is an eraser in British English, something that deletes pencil marks
soul is a genre of music

explanation.surface: Someone wipes out a style of music that The Beatles once put on tape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One deletes' looks like a person, but in Britain a rubber is the eraser on a pencil.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubber Soul is the 1965 studio album by The Beatles, featuring songs such as Norwegian Wood and Michelle.

clue.text: Imbecile deejay losing half computer equipment

indicators.note: losing half means shedding half the letters, so only three of six survive

parts.note: taken as written; three of its six letters go
IT, information technology, covers computer equipment

explanation.surface: A foolish disc jockey loses half of his computer kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half' goes with 'losing', not with the computer equipment: the disc jockey drops three of his six letters, the outer D and the final pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Eejit is an Irish and Scottish colloquial spelling of idiot, a fool or nitwit.

clue.text: One occupied, among trees, fierce boxer without lead

indicators.note: a lead is what goes in front, so going without it drops the opening letter

parts.note: a slogger is a boxer who hits hard rather than skilfully

explanation.surface: A dog lives among the trees: a fierce boxer let off its lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxer' and 'lead' suggest a dog, but the boxer is a hard-hitting fighter, and the lead is its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A logger's job is felling timber, so their working occupation is literally spent in forests and woodland.

clue.text: Own contracting business overcoming disruption

indicators.note: contracting means shrinking, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: to own something is to have it

indicators.note: read as coming over, in a down clue it sends the letters upward, back to front

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a business

explanation.surface: A firm's own building contractors push on through the disruption.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contracting business' looks like a building firm; in fact 'contracting' shortens HAVE, and CO comes over, upward in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Havoc is widespread chaos and devastation, the state of things thrown into severe confusion.

clue.text: Old writer mostly inside leaves alcoholic spirit

indicators.note: inside places one piece within the other

parts.note: tea leaves, so tea

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is cut

parts.note: a quill pen was the old writing instrument

explanation.surface: An elderly author, mostly confined indoors, abandons the bottle of spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old writer' suggests an author, but it is the pen of old; 'leaves' is the brewing kind, not departing.
explanation.definitionFit: Tequila is a Mexican distilled liquor made from blue agave, a classic strong spirit.

clue.text: Man goes to prison for drinking

definitions.note: a phrase describing the noun: a vessel for drinking

parts.note: Toby is a man's name
jug is slang for prison

explanation.surface: A man is sent to jail for drunkenness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For drinking' seems to be the crime, but it defines the answer. Jug is old slang for jail.
explanation.definitionFit: A Toby jug is a pottery beer mug shaped like a seated man in a tricorn hat, used to drink ale.

clue.text: Fleece jumper, the most common in Keswick?

parts.note: a roo, a kangaroo, is a famous jumper
K occurs twice in the word Keswick, more than any other letter

explanation.surface: A woollen jumper, the commonest garment in a Lake District town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleece' and 'jumper' look like knitwear; jumper is the British word for a sweater. Keswick is a market town in England's Lake District, sheep country.
explanation.definitionFit: To fleece and to rook both mean to cheat or swindle someone out of money.

clue.text: Plant-feeding insect ascended VW car

parts.note: rose is the past tense of rise, ascended
the Beetle is Volkswagen's famous small car

explanation.surface: A bug that eats plants climbed up onto a Volkswagen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ascended' looks like a verb in the story, but it supplies a word of its own, the past tense of rise.
explanation.definitionFit: The rose beetle, or rose chafer, is a beetle that eats the leaves and flowers of roses and other garden plants.

clue.text: Resort to fighting, without hesitation, a supermarket that's dodgy

indicators.note: dodgy means unreliable or crooked, so the letters are put out of true
without means lacking, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
er is the sound of hesitating; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: Driven to violence without a second thought by a shady supermarket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without hesitation' reads as 'immediately', but it removes the hesitation sound before the remaining ten letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To take up arms is to pick up weapons and start a fight or war, an idiom for resorting to combat.

clue.text: Soprano greeting academy member with unknown wine

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for soprano
hi is a greeting
an RA is a Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts
in algebra x, y and z are unknowns

explanation.surface: An opera singer greets a fellow of the academy over a glass of mystery wine.
explanation.walkthrough: Four short conventional abbreviations string together; Z as an unknown comes from algebra.
explanation.definitionFit: Shiraz is a red grape variety, also called Syrah, and the full-bodied red made from it.

clue.text: Inside skips, noticed tools

indicators.note: inside puts one piece within the other

parts.note: to jig is to skip or dance lightly
saw is the past of see, noticed

explanation.surface: Someone peering inside rubbish skips spots some tools.
explanation.walkthrough: A skip is a British builder's rubbish container, which makes the surface a scavenging scene; here it is the verb, to jig.
explanation.definitionFit: A jigsaw is a fine-bladed saw for cutting curves, a common workshop power tool.

clue.text: Wife Tessa, confused, wrong about Old English dialect

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for wife

indicators.note: confused means muddled, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
X is the mark for a wrong answer
on means about, concerning

explanation.surface: A muddled wife gets things wrong about early English speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a container signal but is ON, as in 'a book on birds'; 'Old English dialect' is wholly the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: West Saxon, spoken in the kingdom of Wessex, became the standard literary form of Anglo-Saxon writing.

clue.text: Onward into the centre of fabulous African city

indicators.note: going into something means being placed within it
the centre is the middle, so only the inner letters are kept

parts.note: the four central letters of the eight
away, as in 'fire away', means onward or on

explanation.surface: Heading onward into the heart of a marvellous African city.
explanation.walkthrough: The centre is four letters, not one or two, since the word has eight; AWAY fits between L and O.
explanation.definitionFit: Bulawayo is the second-largest city in Zimbabwe, in the south-west of the country.

clue.text: With customary practice, lines like a wordsmith can be created

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for with
a rite is a customary ceremony or practice
RLY abbreviates railway, a set of lines

explanation.surface: Following habit, the lines a poet might produce can be written.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lines' suggests verse, but here railway lines, abbreviated RLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Writerly describes style or qualities characteristic of a professional author, someone skilled with words.

clue.text: Regularly zealous on mountain, cross a group of countries

indicators.note: in an across clue, placed on means coming after the next piece

parts.note: a ben is a Scottish mountain, as in Ben Nevis

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters
X is the shape of a cross

explanation.surface: Keen climbers on a peak cross over into a cluster of nations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' could be angry, but it is the letter shaped like one.
explanation.definitionFit: Benelux is the collective name for Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg, formed from their initial syllables.

clue.text: Heavenly body's attractiveness seen in middle of square

indicators.note: something seen in a place sits inside it
the middle is the central part, so the outer letters are dropped

parts.note: the central four letters of the six
SA stands for sex appeal

explanation.surface: A star's good looks are on display in the town square.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is 'is', linking definition to wordplay. SA for sex appeal is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: A quasar is an extremely luminous, distant galactic nucleus, an astronomical object in the sky.

clue.text: Set up force in company of US agent

indicators.note: being in someone's company means being kept within their party

parts.note: a fed is an American federal agent, e.g. of the FBI
to ram is to force or drive hard

explanation.surface: A police force is set up alongside an American federal agency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Force' seems to be a police force, but it is a verb meaning to ram.
explanation.definitionFit: To be set up is to be framed: incriminated with false evidence for something one did not do.

clue.text: Old-fashioned tone of Private Eye in the main

indicators.note: in places one piece within the other

parts.note: the main is a poetic term for the open sea
a private eye is a private investigator, PI

explanation.surface: The magazine Private Eye has a dated tone in most of its pages.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye is a British satirical magazine, and 'in the main' means mostly; split differently they are a detective and the ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: Sepia is the reddish-brown tint of early photographs, so it evokes a quaint, vintage look.

clue.text: Father, turning over fruit in grass, became visible again

indicators.note: in places those pieces within another

parts.note: a reed is a tall waterside grass

indicators.note: turning over flips something, so its letters run the other way

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father
a pear is a fruit

explanation.surface: Dad, rolling over a piece of fruit in the long grass, popped back into view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' could be British slang for an informer, but here it is a waterside plant; both father and fruit go inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To reappear is to show up once more after being out of sight, so it is coming back into view.

clue.text: Extremists around north joining current soldier

indicators.note: joining means attaching, so the next piece is added on
around means surrounding, so these letters go on either side

parts.note: A and Z are the extremes of the alphabet
N is the abbreviation for north
AC is alternating current

explanation.surface: Radicals from the north sign up with a modern-day soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremists' sounds political, but it means the outermost letters of the alphabet, A and Z.
explanation.definitionFit: An Anzac is a soldier of the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, famous from Gallipoli.

clue.text: During training, sons call for attention

indicators.note: during means within the span of something, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: PT is physical training
S is the abbreviation for son, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: In the middle of a practice session, the boys shout to be noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: PT is gym class at school; two S's for the plural sons fit inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the hissing whisper people use to quietly catch someone's ear without raising their voice.

clue.text: Pop star perhaps disliking work in auditorium

indicators.note: an auditorium is a place for listening, so the sound of the word counts

parts.note: someone who dislikes work is idle

explanation.surface: A lazy pop singer can't be bothered to perform in the concert hall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks a pop star as one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A pop star is a typical example of a teen idol, a celebrity adored by fans.

clue.text: Blue short consumed by Mark before a dance

indicators.note: before means coming first, so the next piece follows on
something consumed is taken inside, so it sits within the other

parts.note: MK is the abbreviation for mark, the old German currency

indicators.note: short means cut off, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: azure is sky blue
taken as written

explanation.surface: Mark, feeling a bit down, drinks before a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue' reads as sad, but it is the colour azure, cut short and placed inside MK.
explanation.definitionFit: The mazurka is a lively Polish folk dance in triple time, made famous in concert halls by Chopin.

clue.text: One creates list at home on RH side, given time off

indicators.note: given time off means sent away, so that letter is removed

parts.note: being in is being at home
dexter is the right-hand side in heraldry

explanation.surface: A person writes a to-do list at home on the right while on leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time off' sounds like a holiday, but it removes T, time. Dexter, Latin for right, is the heraldic right side.
explanation.definitionFit: An indexer compiles the alphabetical index of names and topics at the back of a book.

clue.text: Itinerant shocked by European footwear

indicators.note: an itinerant wanders from place to place, so the letters roam into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A traveller is appalled by a European's choice of shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Itinerant' looks like a noun for the traveller, but it signals that the letters wander.
explanation.definitionFit: A deck shoe is a casual canvas or leather shoe with a non-slip sole, worn by sailors and boaters.

clue.text: Tending to stick Heather in periphery of company

indicators.note: in places one piece within the other
the periphery is the outer edge, so only the end letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters
ling is a common name for heather

explanation.surface: A woman called Heather hovers at the fringes of a group, inclined to hang on.
explanation.walkthrough: Heather looks like a name, but it is the moorland plant, also called ling.
explanation.definitionFit: Clingy describes something that adheres closely, or a person emotionally dependent on others.
